questions.question: What percentage of the total volume of global water is estimated to exist as fresh water?
questions.explanation: According to UN and NCERT hydrological data, approximately 96.5% of the total volume of global water exists in saline oceans and seas, while barely 2.5% exists as fresh water. Of this miniscule 2.5% freshwater reserve, nearly 70% is locked up as permanent continental ice sheets and mountain glaciers in Antarctica, Greenland, and high Himalayan peaks, and slightly under 30% is stored as groundwater in subterranean aquifers. Surface runoff in rivers and freshwater lakes accounts for less than 1% of the planet's total freshwater.

questions.question: Nearly 70 percent of the world's total fresh water occurs as ice sheets and glaciers in:
options: Antarctica, Greenland, and mountain ranges of the world
Underground aquifers of India and China
questions.explanation: Glaciological assessments cited in NCERT Geography demonstrate that out of Earth's tiny 2.5% freshwater endowment, nearly 70% occurs in the form of deep continental ice sheets and mountain glaciers located across Antarctica, Greenland, and the glaciated mountain ranges of the world (including the Himalayas, Andes, and Alps). Consequently, less than 30% of global freshwater is stored in accessible underground aquifers as groundwater, while rivers, streams, and freshwater lakes constitute less than 1% of total accessible liquid freshwater.

questions.question: India receives approximately what percentage of global precipitation, ranking 133 in the world in per capita water availability?
questions.explanation: India receives approximately 4% of total global precipitation annually. However, because India supports nearly 18% of the world's human population on just 2.4% of the global land area, the nation faces severe water stress and ranks 133rd in the world in terms of per capita water availability per annum. Hydrological projections warn that by 2025, vast regions of India containing hundreds of millions of citizens will join nations and territories suffering from absolute water scarcity (availability below 1,000 cubic meters per capita).

questions.question: In India, hydroelectric power contributes approximately what proportion of the total electricity generated?
questions.explanation: According to official Central Electricity Authority and NCERT Geography data, hydroelectric power generation accounts for approximately 22% of India's total electricity production. Multipurpose river valley projects and dedicated hydel stations harness the gravitational kinetic force of river waters through high-head water turbines to generate clean, renewable, and dispatchable electricity, playing an indispensable role in stabilizing the national power grid alongside coal thermal stations and emerging renewable solar/wind installations.

questions.question: Who proudly proclaimed multi-purpose river dams as the 'Temples of Modern India'?
questions.explanation: India's first Prime Minister, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, proudly proclaimed multipurpose river valley projects as the 'Temples of Modern India'. He passionately believed that grand engineering complexes like the Bhakra Nangal and Damodar Valley projects would integrate agricultural development (by supplying controlled irrigation to drought-prone rural hinterlands) with rapid urban industrialisation (by providing abundant hydroelectric power and water supplies to factories, steel mills, and growing industrial cities).

questions.question: The Bhakra-Nangal multipurpose project is constructed on which river basin?
questions.explanation: The Bhakra-Nangal multipurpose project is constructed across the Satluj-Beas river basin in northern India. Featuring the colossal Bhakra concrete gravity dam (one of the highest gravity dams in the world at 226 meters) and the downstream Nangal barrage, it impounds the vast Gobind Sagar reservoir. The project provides both hydroelectric generation (over 1,300 MW) and an extensive network of irrigation canals that revolutionized agricultural productivity across Punjab, Haryana, and arid northern Rajasthan (Indira Gandhi Canal).

questions.question: The Hirakud project, which integrates conservation of water with flood control, is built across which river in Odisha?
questions.explanation: The Hirakud multipurpose project is constructed across the Mahanadi River in Sambalpur district, Odisha. Built as one of the earliest post-independence river valley initiatives, Hirakud features the world's longest composite earthen dam spanning 25.8 kilometers across the valley. The project integrates multiple vital objectives: it provides flood mitigation for the flood-prone Mahanadi coastal delta, generates 347 MW of hydroelectricity, and irrigates hundreds of thousands of hectares of paddy fields across western and coastal Odisha.

questions.question: The Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over which major river in Gujarat?
questions.explanation: The Sardar Sarovar Dam is a colossal concrete gravity dam constructed across the Narmada River near Navagam in Gujarat. It is one of the largest water resources projects in India, designed with an installed hydroelectric capacity of 1,450 MW and a massive 9,490-kilometer canal distribution network. The project was engineered to deliver drinking water and irrigation to 1.8 million hectares of land across 9,490 drought-prone villages and 173 urban townships in Gujarat, as well as barren tracts of Barmer and Jalore in southern Rajasthan.

questions.question: Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save Narmada Movement) is an NGO-led social movement that mobilized tribal people, farmers, and human rights activists primarily against the:
questions.explanation: Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save Narmada Movement) is an environmental Non-Governmental Organisation (NGO) mobilized by Medha Patkar, Baba Amte, tribal adivasis, farmers, and human rights activists against the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River in Gujarat. The movement initially organized mass peaceful resistance against the submergence of vast biodiversity-rich forests and the forced displacement of over 250,000 riparian villagers without proper democratic rehabilitation, later advocating for sustainable decentralized water harvesting.

questions.question: In the hill and mountain regions of the Western Himalayas, people built diversion channels for agricultural irrigation known as:
questions.explanation: In the rugged hill and mountain terrain of the Western Himalayas (particularly in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Ladakh's Spiti Valley), traditional communities developed ingenious diversion channels known locally as 'guls' or 'kuls'. These narrow gravity-fed canals tap glacial meltwater streams and mountain torrents high up on mountain slopes, contouring around steep ridges to lead water gently down into terraced agricultural fields and village community storage tanks for high-altitude apple orchards and barley cultivation.

questions.question: In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly in Bikaner, Phalodi, and Barmer, drinking water is traditionally stored in underground tanks called:
questions.explanation: In the arid and semi-arid regions of Rajasthan (notably in Phalodi, Bikaner, and Barmer), virtually every traditional home historically featured an underground stone or masonry cistern known as a 'tanka'. These subterranean tanks, often as large as a bedroom (e.g., 6.1 meters deep, 4.27 meters long, and 2.44 meters wide), were built inside the central courtyard or under rooms. They were connected by sloping pipes to the clean sloping roofs of houses to harvest, filter, and store every precious drop of summer monsoon rainfall.

questions.question: In arid Rajasthan, pure stored rainwater harvested in underground tankas is considered the purest form of natural water and locally known as:
questions.explanation: In arid Rajasthan, pure harvested rainwater collected from sloping roofs and sealed inside underground masonry tankas is revered as 'Palar pani'. Local communities regard palar pani as the purest, cleanest form of natural potable water on Earth, far superior to salty, mineralized groundwater. Furthermore, storing large volumes of cold palar pani inside underground chambers beneath living quarters cools the ambient temperature of adjoining rooms, providing vital relief during blistering 45°C+ summer desert heatwaves.

questions.question: In arid and semi-arid agricultural regions of Rajasthan, rain-fed storage structures built to collect water and moisten the soil are known as:
options: 'Khadins' in Jaisalmer and 'Johads' in other parts
questions.explanation: In the arid and semi-arid agricultural tracts of Rajasthan, traditional agrarian communities built rain-fed storage structures consisting of long earthen embankment bunds across agricultural slopes. These structures are known as 'Khadins' in Jaisalmer and 'Johads' in other parts of Rajasthan (such as Alwar). The earthen bunds impound seasonal surface runoff during monsoon rains, allowing water to soak deep into the soil and saturate the ground, enabling farmers to cultivate fertile rabi winter crops like wheat and mustard without wells.

questions.question: A 200-year-old traditional system of tapping stream and spring water using bamboo pipes to drip water at the roots of plants is practiced in which state?
questions.explanation: In Meghalaya, tribal farmers (particularly Khasi and Jaintia communities) have practiced an ingenious 200-year-old indigenous water engineering system known as 'bamboo drip irrigation'. Using interconnected bamboo pipes of varying diameters, stream and spring water from uphill ridges is tapped and transported across hundreds of meters over rugged terrain and gorges. By carefully adjusting pipe slopes, inflow is reduced from 18–20 liters per minute at the source down to 20–80 precision drops per minute directly at roots of betel vines.

questions.question: Which is the first state in India that has made rooftop rainwater harvesting structure compulsory for all houses across the state, with legal punishment for defaulters?
questions.explanation: Tamil Nadu is the pioneering first state in India to make rooftop rainwater harvesting (RWH) legally compulsory for all residential, commercial, and institutional buildings across the state. Under landmark amendments to the Tamil Nadu District Municipalities Act in 2001, every building must install compliant rooftop catchment and recharge structures (percolation pits or storage tanks). Defaulting premises face punitive legal consequences, including the immediate disconnection of municipal drinking water and sewerage connections.

questions.question: In which remote village of Mysuru (Karnataka) have villagers installed rooftop rainwater harvesting systems in nearly 200 households, earning the distinction of being rich in rainwater?
questions.explanation: Gendathur, a remote agricultural village in Mysuru district of Karnataka, achieved national and global acclaim for community water conservation. Nearly 200 households installed standardized rooftop rainwater harvesting systems on their roofs. Each house harvests up to 50,000 to 1,00,000 liters of pristine rainwater annually from an average 1,000 mm of annual rainfall across 20 filling cycles, replenishing community wells and providing over 10 lakh liters of pure water annually, earning Gendathur the rare title of a 'water-rich village'.

questions.question: In the flood plains of Bengal, how did traditional farmers irrigate their agricultural fields without causing waterlogging?
options: By developing inundation canals to channel floodwaters onto crop fields
By digging deep tubewells into the seabed
questions.explanation: In the flood plains of Bengal, traditional farmers developed an ecological irrigation system of 'inundation canals'. During seasonal monsoon flooding of the Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems, farmers cut temporary breach channels through natural river levees to lead silt-laden floodwaters directly into low-lying agricultural fields. This ingenious indigenous system served a dual ecological purpose: it thoroughly irrigated paddy crops and deposited fresh, nutrient-rich alluvium across the fields while washing away agricultural pests.

questions.question: In the first century BC, an extraordinary water harvesting system channeling the floodwaters of the River Ganga was built at:
questions.explanation: Archaeological excavations at Sringaverapura near Prayagraj (Allahabad), Uttar Pradesh, revealed an extraordinary water harvesting and hydraulic engineering complex dating back to the first century BC. The ancient engineers constructed a sophisticated brick-lined canal network connected to the Ganga River. During high monsoon floods, water was diverted through a deep intake channel into a large silting chamber that slowed velocity and precipitated heavy sediment, before cascading filtered clean water into circular storage reservoirs.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Geography, Chapter 3, Section 2, Box

questions.question: One of the largest artificial lakes of its time, built in the eleventh century in central India, was:
questions.explanation: Bhopal Lake (historically known as Upper Lake or Bhojtal) is one of the largest and oldest artificial freshwater lakes in medieval India, constructed in the eleventh century during the reign of Paramara King Bhoja (1005–1055 AD). Built by erecting massive stone masonry dams across the Kolans River, the sprawling reservoir covers an area of approximately 31 square kilometers, providing flood control, groundwater recharge, and an uninterrupted supply of potable water that continues to sustain the historical city of Bhopal today.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Geography, Chapter 3, Section 2, Box

questions.question: In the fourteenth century, which Delhi Sultan constructed the tank at Hauz Khas to supply water to the Siri Fort area?
questions.explanation: In the fourteenth century, Sultan Shamsuddin Iltutmish (the third ruler of the Delhi Mamluk Sultanate) constructed the celebrated grand water reservoir tank known as the Hauz Khas (originally named Hauz-i-Shamsi) in Delhi. Engineered with lime-plastered stone masonry, the expansive reservoir was designed to capture monsoon runoff from the surrounding Aravalli ridges to provide an uninterrupted, reliable supply of potable water for the royal court and the imperial army garrison stationed at the fortified city of Siri Fort.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Geography, Chapter 3, Section 2, Box
